entries.content: Shane Kanterman is a Computer Science student at Southern Connecticut State University, expected to complete the program in May 2027, and a current Data Center Technician at InterServer since June 2025. He is also an active member of the university football program. His public portfolio focuses on Linux platforms, server provisioning, networking, deployment tooling, ephemeral CI, and self-hosted infrastructure. He has experience with building servers and hardware modifications, rack-and-stack work, Linux administration, server deployment, decommissioning, hardware troubleshooting, and practical software delivery, including a recent data center deployment buildout of roughly 72 racks, racked and wired end to end. The portfolio lists a Technical Support Fundamentals certificate from Google/Coursera (June 2025). Outside InterServer he founded and operates KanterLabs, an independent product and infrastructure studio whose public projects are on GitHub at github.com/KanterLabs. His lead project is Helm, a self-hosted project board and bug tracker where people and software agents move work together.

For professional inquiries, the public portfolio contact section lists Shane's email address: shanekanterman04@gmail.com. That section also links his LinkedIn profile, the KanterLabs GitHub organization (github.com/KanterLabs), where his public projects live, and his personal GitHub profile.

KanterLabs is the independent product and infrastructure studio Shane founded and operates. It builds developer tools, self-hosted platforms, and practical software, together with the infrastructure to run them, and its public repositories are at github.com/KanterLabs. The portfolio lists 12 public projects. Helm is the lead project: a Go and Svelte self-hosted project board and bug tracker where people and software agents move work together, with scoped agent tokens and an auditable API (v0.1.0, with a case study). Other flagships: ActionView (GNOME Shell extension showing the KanterLabs self-hosted GitHub Actions runner fleet), NFL Scores (GNOME Shell extension with live scores and a drawn-on-the-field gamecast), Zeus OS (a Fedora bootc laptop desktop, 0.1 preview), and Greenlit (Rust tool for running GitHub Actions workflows locally, pre-release). Other public projects: Zeus Code (terminal workspace for Codex and OpenCode conversations), Linkshare (Go link inbox for a person and their coding agents), Pulse (GNOME Spotify command center, pre-alpha), an ncspot fork, RunComp (running-competition app with private groups, streaks, weekly challenges, and push alerts), Patchwork Pirates (co-op roguelite in pre-production), and this portfolio's source.

The portfolio groups Shane's capabilities into systems and networking, platform and delivery, and software and data. Publicly listed tools include Linux, Proxmox, Nginx, Caddy, Cloudflare, Tailscale, PXE Boot, GitHub Actions, k3s, Actions Runner Controller, Docker, GHCR, atomic releases, Rust, TypeScript, Next.js, Python, PostgreSQL, Git, and Astro. His architecture work emphasizes clear ingress boundaries, isolated workloads, ephemeral CI runners, health checks, atomic releases, and retained rollback paths.

Helm is Shane's lead KanterLabs project: a small, self-hosted project board and bug tracker where people and software agents move work together. People use a Svelte and TypeScript Kanban board with Focus, My work, Live Work, and Roadmap views; agents use the same versioned Go REST API (/api/v1, described by an OpenAPI document) with their own hashed, project-scoped bearer tokens. Agents claim tasks as renewable leases, post live progress, and follow a cursor-based event feed; a claimed task with no update for 15 minutes is marked stale. Every mutation uses ETag/If-Match optimistic concurrency and idempotency keys so retries are safe, and board audits are read-only until someone confirms a recommendation. It runs as one unprivileged container with a read-only root filesystem on a single SQLite (WAL) database, supports local accounts, Cloudflare Access, or a private Tailnet mode, and ships an installable Codex skill. Helm v0.1.0 is the first public release; Shane runs it in production on the KanterLabs homelab, deployed through a private beta with signed SHA-tagged releases, verified pre-upgrade backups, schema preflight, and rollback. The production instance is private.

The KanterLabs Homelab Platform turns a small collection of systems into an intentional two-site platform. Its public case study describes hardened edge VMs at both sites, distinct management, ingress, public-origin, and private-origin planes, exact service listeners, split-horizon private DNS, verified edge-to-origin TLS, and default-deny network policy. Public traffic uses dedicated Cloudflare paths, while named Tailscale services provide private entrances without direct workload-network access. Network changes use deterministic configuration, timed rollback, independent management checks, synthetic canaries, and negative exposure tests. GitHub Actions jobs run in disposable pods managed by Actions Runner Controller, with secrets kept outside Git.

The Dual-Origin Portfolio Deployment case study describes a static Astro portfolio delivered as the same immutable release to OVH and homelab Nginx origins. Cloudflare provides public TLS, health checks, and production load balancing. GitHub Actions deploys beta artifacts directly over private management paths to both isolated candidate lanes. After beta merges to main, the workflow stages and privately verifies the tested main artifact on both origins, then automatically promotes that exact digest to production with coordinated rollback. The design separates public ingress, private deployment, and workload responsibilities while retaining commit-addressed releases for recovery.

Shane's InterServer Data Center Technician experience covers building servers, hardware modifications and upgrades, rack-and-stack, cabling and wiring, Linux, Windows and Proxmox installation, inventory checks, hardware diagnostics, failed-drive and memory troubleshooting, NIC and boot troubleshooting, decommissioning retired systems, and deployment documentation. More recently the work has included a full deployment buildout: roughly 72 racks stood up inside a data center and wired end to end, covering rack layout, power and network runs, labeling, and staged build order at scale. He is also experienced with PXE-based network-boot imaging from doing it at volume, though it is background depth rather than a current day-to-day task. The case study emphasizes evidence-based diagnosis, deliberate sequencing, communication, repeatable patterns, and operational care around live infrastructure.
